summary: Jesus compares the kingdom to a tiny mustard seed that becomes a tree and to leaven hidden in flour until the whole batch rises.
key_insight: Both parables begin with something almost invisible: a seed smaller than all the seeds, leaven a woman “hid” in the flour. Both end in fullness: birds nesting in the branches, the meal “all leavened.” The small start is part of the picture, not a problem in it.
story: Jesus asked the crowd, “To what shall we liken the kingdom of God? Or with what parable shall we picture it?” {Mk}

It is like a mustard seed which a man took and sowed in his field. {Mt} When it is sown, it is smaller than all the seeds on earth. But it grows up, becomes greater than all the garden plants and shoots out large branches, {Mk} until it becomes a tree, “so that the birds of the air come and nest in its branches.” {Mt}
He gave them another picture: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal till it was all leavened.”

With many such parables He spoke the word to them as they were able to hear it. {Mk} He did not speak to the crowds without a parable, fulfilling what the prophet had said: “I will open My mouth in parables; I will utter things kept secret from the foundation of the world.” {Mt} But when He was alone with His disciples, He explained all things to them. {Mk}

On another occasion, a Sabbath when Jesus had healed a woman bent over for eighteen years in a synagogue, He asked again, “What is the kingdom of God like? And to what shall I compare it?” Once more He spoke of a mustard seed that a man “put in his garden,” which “became a large tree,” and of leaven hidden in three measures of meal. {Lk}
differences: Matthew and Luke give both the mustard seed and the leaven; Mark gives only the mustard seed.
The seed is sown “in his field” (Matthew), “on the ground” (Mark) and “in his garden” (Luke).
Matthew and Luke say it became a tree with birds nesting “in its branches”; Mark says it shoots out large branches so the birds “may nest under its shade.”
Only Matthew quotes the psalm about opening the mouth in parables; only Mark says Jesus explained everything privately to His disciples.
Luke sets these parables after a Sabbath healing in a synagogue (Luke 13:10–21), not beside the Sea of Galilee.

fit.question: Matthew and Mark place these parables by the Sea of Galilee. Luke places them after a Sabbath healing in a synagogue, on Jesus’ later journey. Which setting is right?

points.label: Told more than once
points.text: Luke links the parables to the synagogue scene with “Then He said” (13:18), right after the crowd rejoiced at the healing. A traveling teacher would naturally use short, memorable pictures like these in more than one place. Mark says Jesus spoke “many such parables.”

points.label: Luke’s arrangement
points.text: If this was one occasion, Luke may have set the parables where they shed light on his story: the kingdom growing in power while Jesus’ opponents were put to shame (13:17).

fit.note: Whether Jesus told these parables twice or Luke arranged them by theme, each Gospel reports His words truthfully.
fit.short: Jesus may have told these short parables more than once, or Luke placed them by theme after a later Sabbath healing.

scene.label: The mustard seed
scene.text: Black mustard was sown in fields and gardens around the Sea of Galilee. Its seed was proverbially tiny (Matthew 17:20), the smallest seed a Galilean farmer sowed, yet the plant can grow taller than a man, ten feet or more, in a single season.

scene.label: Birds in the branches
scene.text: The prophets pictured great kingdoms as trees where birds nest (Ezekiel 17:23; 31:6; Daniel 4:12). Jesus’ hearers would catch the echo.

scene.label: Leaven
scene.text: Leaven was a lump of old fermented dough saved from the last baking and worked into the new. A small piece spread quietly through the whole batch.

scene.label: Three measures
scene.text: Three measures of meal was a very large baking, enough bread for a crowd. It is the amount Abraham asked Sarah to prepare for the three visitors at Mamre (Genesis 18:6).

scene.label: The psalm
scene.text: Matthew quotes Psalm 78:2, a psalm of Asaph, whom Scripture calls “the seer” (2 Chronicles 29:30). The psalm retells Israel’s history to bring out its hidden lessons.

witnesses.matthew: Pairs a man’s seed with a woman’s leaven, work in the field with work in the kitchen, and adds the psalm to show that Jesus’ way of teaching fulfills Scripture. These two parables close the public part of Matthew 13 before Jesus goes into the house.
witnesses.mark: Tells only the mustard seed and closes his section of parables with a summary: Jesus spoke to the crowds “as they were able to hear it,” and explained everything privately to His disciples. Mark’s seed grows until birds “may nest under its shade,” a picture of shelter.
witnesses.luke: Places both parables right after a synagogue ruler protested a Sabbath healing and the crowd rejoiced at Jesus’ works (13:14–17). In Luke the kingdom is already pushing back against opposition as Jesus journeys toward Jerusalem.

seeing.reveals: Jesus is the King whose kingdom begins in weakness: a carpenter from Nazareth, twelve ordinary men and, soon, a cross. Yet He speaks with complete confidence that His kingdom will fill the world.
seeing.living: Do not judge the kingdom’s future by its size today. Jesus works through small and hidden things, a seed in a field or leaven in dough, and He works thoroughly. Give Him the hidden corners of your life as well as the public ones, and let His word work its way through all of it.
seeing.ponder: Where have you dismissed what God is doing because it looked too small to matter?

preaching.big_idea: The kingdom starts small and hidden, but it will fill everything.
preaching.watch_for: Leaven usually pictures corruption in Scripture (Matthew 16:6; 1 Corinthians 5:6–8), so some read this parable as a warning about evil spreading in the visible church. Most read it, with its twin the mustard seed, as the kingdom’s hidden and complete growth; both open with “The kingdom of heaven is like.”
